stories.headline: Snapping ties abruptly with a match made in heaven
stories.deck: When he dismissed Kent’s Zimbabwean batter Tawanda Muyeye for his third scalp of the innings and his 50th of the season on September 15, James Anderson would hardly have imagined that it would be his final wicket for Lancashire
stories.bodyText:
In one fell swoop, without warning or indication, without even a hint of what was coming, a 26-year-old association was snapped in a jiffy. Inarguably the greatest son of the soil was let go without so much as a thank you, a decision that has so infuriated members and supporters that the ‘offending’ party is now contemplating a formal farewell to celebrate the life and times of Test cricket’s most prolific wicket-taker among fast bowlers.
When he dismissed Kent’s Zimbabwean batter Tawanda Muyeye for his third wicket of the innings and his 50th of the season on September 15, James Anderson would hardly have imagined that it would be his final wicket-taking contribution to Lancashire. Having taken over the captaincy of the embattled county towards the middle of the 2025 season, he was appointed full-time skipper in the season gone by.
Fabulous campaign
Personally, it was another fabulous campaign for the 44-year-old king of swing, whose 50 wickets came at the fantastic average of 17.68. But the team spiralled from one disaster to another, finishing second from last in Division Two, its worst-ever Championship finish.
Incoming director of cricket Paul Farbrace, who has ambitiously charted out a four-year time-frame to return the county to its glory days, and recently appointed chief executive Richard Kenyon have held forth on the need to rebuild the stuttering outfit and clearly, they feel that despite plenty of fight still left in Anderson, he doesn’t exactly figure in their immediate long-term plans.
Anderson became superfluous to England’s scheme of things under Ben Stokes and Brendon McCullum in July 2024 when he was ushered into retirement after the Lord’s Test against West Indies. At the time, he had expressed the desire to play on for another three years, assuming blithely — and justifiably — that he would wind down his First Class career with the team he had served outstandingly for so long. Unfortunately, that was not to be after the county decided to sever ties with the champion who took 443 First Class wickets, 83 List A scalps and 50 T20 wickets in 213 matches across formats.
Even in the short interlude since Lancashire’s dramatic and largely unpopular call, several counties have started weighing up their options because they believe that even when he is 45, which he will turn midway through next season, Anderson still is far from a spent force or a liability. But while Anderson hasn’t yet invoked the R (retirement) word, it’s hard to see him switching allegiance at this late stage of his career. Anderson made his displeasure at the call apparent without launching into an all-out attack, saying in a statement, “If it was up to me, it wouldn’t have ended like this, but I wish the players and fans all the best for the future.” But sadly, it wasn’t up to him, and so this is how it has ended.
One hopes that when the emotions settle down, both parties concerned will be able to look back at the long-standing relationship with fondness and nostalgia. Anderson cut his teeth with Lancashire as a 17-year-old in 2000, made his First Class debut in 2002 and was playing One-Day International cricket that same year. His Test debut came in May 2003, also at Lord’s where he made his final appearance for his country, and from then on, he became one of the most valued members of the five-day squad, striking up an excellent relationship with that other great England pacer of his generation, Stuart Broad.
Easy, repeatable action
A master of swing who went on and on because of his easy, repeatable action that seemingly put very little strain on his body, Anderson was at his most prolific at home, of course, but it wasn’t as if he struggled to adapt to the challenges of the subcontinent where, more than anywhere else, overseas quicks have struggled to make an impact. Towards the later stages of his career, he developed the scrambled-seam delivery that brought him great success, but for the large part, especially but not only with the new ball, he was the master of having the ball on a string and making it go this way and that with a gentle tug here, a little pull there.
An overwhelming majority of his 704 Test wickets came on home turf – 438, which accounted for 62.22% of all his successes in the five-day game – but that’s also because he played 106 of his 188 Tests in England. For a fast bowler to continue on for 21 years at the highest level and average nearly nine Tests a year is little short of staggering; it speaks to not just his fitness levels and his propensity to take excellent care of his body, but also to his commitment and hunger and fire and passion, traits that aren’t necessarily the most prominent in an era where shelf-lives are getting increasingly shorter and the lure of the 20-over shootout is almost impossible to resist.
Anderson was at his most comfortable with the Duke’s ball in his right hand, a ball he practically grew up with, though he showed his felicity with the Kookaburra used in most other parts of the world. Across Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, he snaffled 138 wickets in 40 matches, not in the out-of-the-world category but definitely numbers that exploded the myth that he was a home bully. He also had decent success in India with the SG Test which he isn’t all that familiar with – 17 Tests across 18 years fetched him 44 wickets. On his last tour of India in February-March 2024, he grabbed 10 wickets in four outings, gatecrashing into the hitherto exclusive 700-club of Muttiah Muralitharan and Shane Warne in the scenic surrounds of Dharamshala in the final Test of a five-match series that the hosts bossed 4-1.
In perfect harmony
Anderson in action wasn’t unlike poetry in motion, with his unhurried and visibly inexplosive run-up and perfect harmony between the operative body parts as he slotted into his delivery stride. It wasn’t as if he didn’t have bad days, but they were so few and far between as to fall in the ‘hen’s teeth’ section. When the conditions favoured him, he got the ball to whoop around corners, but even when there wasn’t much help on offer, he was still a perennial threat because he was always at the batters, giving them not a moment’s respite.
That he didn’t lose his swing even for a short period over such an extended timeframe at the top level is tribute to his perseverance and humility. Sometimes, it is easy to get carried away with what might appear to be a God-given gift but which needs to be honed and polished and worked on assiduously, day after day, practice session after training stint. Anderson knew he was special, but he also knew that to take that for granted would come with terrible repercussions. Hence the constant quest to keep improving, to keep becoming a better version of himself, to keep plugging away at the nets and in game situations, so that he did not remain static while the world moved ahead of him.
In so many ways, England’s decision to disassociate themselves from Anderson after the disastrous 2015 50-over World Cup campaign proved to be a masterstroke. After their first-round elimination — defeat to Bangladesh pulled the rug from under their feet and ensured that they didn’t even make it to the quarterfinals despite eight teams advancing to the knockouts — England’s bosses got together and arrived at the conclusion that they needed to be smart about how they went about their business. There was a distinct slant towards all-rounders (not just utility players like Mark Ealham and Ronnie Irani and their likes in the mid-1990s), which meant alongside Broad, Anderson was put out to pasture.
Collateral damage
Anderson’s ODI numbers at the stage were anything but ordinary — 269 wickets in 194 matches, economy 4.92, a wicket every six overs — but he was collateral damage as a new-age mentality took deep root under Eoin Morgan’s captaincy. Who’s to say that the Morgan philosophy was flawed, given that England, finally, clinched the World Cup on home patch in 2019 even though they didn’t actually beat New Zealand on the field in the final, either in regulation time or in the Super Over, both of which ended with scores level.
Anderson had bowled close to 1,600 overs in ODIs by March 2015, and though he pulled the plug on his List A career in 2019, the T20 challenge was something he was willing to take on head-on. In what has since become his final season with Lancashire, he figured in the domestic T20 blast, mostly fastidiously parsimonious even if, in his final 20-over outing for the county, he ended up conceding 50 runs in his four overs in the 22-run defeat of bitter rivals Yorkshire in the War of the Roses.
Because the next county season isn’t until another six months from now, one might get the impression that Anderson has some time before deciding on his next course of action. Only he can say with certainty if he is contemplating a change of counties, if only for one final hurrah; the most dramatic script will entail him taking a bagful of wickets against his old home and bowling his new side to the most comprehensive of victories, but such fairytale scripts seldom play out in real life.
The big call ahead of him is whether he is game to give it one more shot from an unfamiliar dressing room after having spent all his professional career with Lancs since his maiden appearance as a teenager. Whether he swings in that direction remains to be seen. What is beyond question is the magnificence of his craft, the joy he brought so many with his command and control, his prime position in the pantheon of cricketing greats and the almost iron-clad certainty that he will remain the only fast bowler in the 700-wicket club in Test cricket for a long, long time to come.

briefs.headline: Ranji Trophy: Shorey, Samarth, Malewar fifties put Vidarbha in pole position
briefs.deck: The home team wraaps up the Goan first innings for 220
briefs.bodyText:
R. Samarth (53, 122b, 5x4), Dhruv Shorey (63, 127b, 5x4), and Danish Malewar (51, 86b, 7x4) helped Vidarbha extend its dominance on the second day of its Ranji Trophy Elite Group- A match against Goa at the VCA Jamtha Stadium here on Tuesday.
Vidarbha came into the day needing two wickets to wrap up Goa’s first innings, and it did so inside the first hour. Rajneesh Gurbani quickly nicked off Vasuki Koushik, leaving Yash Kasvankar the final recognised batter.
Kasvankar played aggressively, but before he could add much, Nachiket Bhute bounced out Shubam Tari, earning him his fifth wicket and ending Goa’s first essay.
Koushik and Ruthvik Naik maintained a consistent line and length for Goa, denying openers Aman Mokhade and Satyam Bhoye easy scoring options, and their frugality accounted for Bhoye, who offered a catch off Koushik.
Mokhade and Samarth together stitched a stabilizing partnership, parking overt aggression for a more watchful eye to reach the Lunch break.
The duo looked to accelerate after the interval, but Mokhade brought about his own downfall by fiddling at a delivery in the channel from Ruthvik. His dismissal proved no distraction to Samarth though, who continued to accumulate steadily with Shorey for company.
Samarth eventually raised his fifty with a hook, but the same shot nearly proved his downfall only for wicketkeeper Shivendra Bhujbal to shell a simple chance. That luck did not repeat when he feathered one from his former Karnataka teammate Koushik behind.
Samarth was replaced at the crease by Malewar, who opted for a more proactive approach from the get-go. As the light slowly faded away, Shorey punched Kasvankar to long-on to complete a half-century, while Malewar raised his first fifty of the season with a punch down the ground of Misal in the day’s final over.

briefs.headline: Young javelin star Dharanidharan eyes breaching the 80m mark
briefs.deck: Dharanidharan began his journey with the pole vault in Class IX before financial difficulties forced him to switch to javelin the following year
briefs.bodyText:
An unusually large crowd — cheering, clapping and whistling — greeted the finalists in the under-20 men’s javelin as the curtain came down on the 41st National junior athletics championships at the Nehru Stadium in Chennai on Tuesday (October 27, 2026). Among them — a youngster from Thanjavur.
A purposeful sprint down the runway, followed by a clean release, saw Dharanidharan open with a throw of 75.34m.
However, second time’s the charm. A huge roar just before his run-up, followed by a powerful sprint and a clean release, saw the spear sail through the air before landing at 76.18m. The crowd erupted, for Dharanidharan had just produced the throw that would fetch him gold.
He followed it with another effort of 75.37m, making it three successive throws beyond 75m.
Despite winning gold, Dharanidharan had hoped for more. He had come with a target of 80m and was disappointed at not being able to achieve it.
“My aim and goal were different. I really thought I would breach 80m,” said the second-year student at Loyola College, who hails from Papanadu in Thanjavur district.
Valuable experience
Having finished sixth at the World U-20 Championships in Eugene, USA, in August, the youngster said the experience of competing against some of the best athletes had helped him improve.
“There were world-class athletes there, and I learned a lot from them,” he said.
Interestingly, Dharanidharan began his journey with the pole vault in Class IX before financial difficulties forced him to switch to javelin the following year.
His coach Manikandan, who trains him in Thanjavur, was pleased with his progress.
“We were aiming for 78 to 80 metres. I was confident he could throw 78m at least. He has improved by around three metres in two months, and that is purely because of his hard work and changes to his technique,” said Manikandan.
The coach also felt that improving his strength and power would be crucial as Dharanidharan looks to take the next step.
For Dharanidharan, though, the focus is on the upcoming season, when he hopes to breach the 80m mark and perhaps even rewrite the record books.

briefs.headline: Ranji Trophy: Salil takes Punjab to 431; Hyderabad solid in reply
briefs.deck: The middle-order batter smashes his third successive ton and puts on 116 for the last wicket with Umesh after Milind reduces the visitor to 315 for nine; Abhirath and Rahul lead the host’s response
briefs.bodyText:
Hyderabad held what looked like a winning hand: a bouncer that did its work, a sharp catch at slip and nine Punjab wickets in the bag. Salil Arora then held his nerve and Umesh Yadav offered a straight bat.
By the time the cards were turned, Salil recorded his highest First Class score (151, 268b, 11x4, 4x6) and Punjab finished on 431 in a Ranji Trophy clash at the Gymkhana Ground on Tuesday.
Hyderabad, anchored by Abhirath Reddy and Raul Radesh’s 259-ball 154-run stand, ended the day on 193 for two.
Earlier, the home side began with a flourish, courtesy C.V. Milind. Emanjot Singh fell first and Harjas Singh followed, undone by a bouncer. Harpreet Brar was then trapped leg-before and by the 45th minute into day two, Punjab was 315 for nine.
A century for Salil, batting on 73, looked a far cry when Umesh joined him. What followed was a last-wicket resistance.
Umesh dug in, content to defend, while Salil inched towards the 90s.
Then, Salil cut loose, launching the ball over long-off. That urgency nearly cost him, when a straight drive fell agonisingly short of Abhirath. Unfazed, He brought up his third consecutive century this season with a maximum over extra cover.
Umesh, playing second fiddle until then, smashed a six and two fours off Varun Goud, announcing a change of gears.
Salil went past 150 before Rakshann Readdi breached his defences to end the 154-ball 116-run stand heading into lunch. Umesh remained unbeaten on 37 (56b, 3x4, 3x6).
Hyderabad was pegged back before it could settle, Tanmay Agarwal’s flick flying straight to Jashanpreet Singh Sidhu at short-leg. Abhirath and Rahul, understandably, batted with some caution.
Their patient approach was rewarded with fifties: Abhirath getting to the milestone off 75 balls while Rahul got there in 105.
Abhirath, however, fell agonisingly short of a century when Salil produced a low, diving catch. By stumps, Hyderabad trailed Punjab by 238 runs.

briefs.headline: India likely to experiment in final ODI
briefs.deck: The Women in Blue are aiming for a clean sweep against the Zimbabweans
briefs.bodyText:
The series may be sealed and a much-needed break is calling out for both India and Zimbabwe before their next international assignments, but there’s still a One-Day encounter left to bring the curtains down on this historic tour at the BCA Stadium here on Wednesday.
The host, with two massive wins, has every reason to experiment without fear. After a day’s break where cafes were visited, friends were met and last-minute shopping lists were ticked off, the Indian team had a full training session under the hot afternoon sun with local security and venue staff keenly watching how Baroda girl Yastika Bhatia — yet to feature in this series — was coming along in the nets.
Harmanpreet Kaur, who has been dealing with a fever for a few days including when she scored her sensational hundred in the second fixture, also had some light hits against the sight-screen before launching a few big shots straight down the ground in the nets.
But the bowling line-up, with its inability to strike as frequently as it might like, has posed a few tough questions to the think-tank. If workload calculations work in her favour, India might want to consider handing seamer Nandani Sharma her India cap.
With a testing multi-format tour of South Africa coming up in December, India will want to get any last minute trials out of the way here.
Zimbabwe players, meanwhile, snuck a trip to the Statue of Unity, around 90km away from Vadodara, while a few like the big-hitting Sharne Mayers — who missed the second game due to a groin strain – stayed back to complete recovery.
The Lady Chevrons have their task cut out. They are yet to get to the 50-over finish line, falling short valiantly by barely a few balls. The side also has the 230-250 mark as a box to tick and will hope to end its India sojourn on a high.

briefs.headline: Salil credits coaches Rajan and Yuvraj for his purple patch
briefs.deck: Salil’s crucial 93-run stand with Ramandeep on day one and his 116-run 10th-wicket partnership with Umesh on Tuesday take the wind out of Hyderabad’s sails
briefs.bodyText:
Two men, one franchise, one mentor. Both don Sunrisers Hyderabad colours, and carry Yuvraj Singh’s lessons to the crease.
Both scored centuries on Tuesday, but in different languages: one in the staccato verse of international cricket’s shortest format, the other in the slow, unhurried prose of the longest on the domestic circuit.
While Abhishek Sharma’s blitzkrieg set New Zealand ablaze, about 11,800 kilometres away at the Gymkhana, Salil Arora laid his knock stone by stone – his fourth and highest First-Class ton – to help Punjab rise above Hyderabad.
Salil’s crucial 93-run stand with Ramandeep Singh on day one and his 116-run 10th-wicket partnership with Umesh Yadav on Tuesday took the wind out of Hyderabad’s sails.
The 23-year-old credited his coach, Rajan Gill, and Yuvraj for a Ranji purple patch that has seen him register three centuries on the trot to sit fourth on the runs table.
“After the IPL, I played district matches back home. I then got a few months to work with the red ball. I practised with my coach in Amritsar for almost a month and a half. After that, I got a call from Yuvraj Singh and batted with him for a week,” he told The Hindu.
“I had problems with my technique last year. Making tweaks to that in Amritsar has given me a lot of benefit.”
Salil is no stranger to the City of Pearls.
“Hyderabad feels like home. I’m here for three to four months (during IPL). So it feels good to get 150 here. The team needed it. I thought if I play till the end, we’ll be able to score 400. I was just playing according to the merit of the ball and to the situation.”
“Yes, it’s a flat wicket. The batters did their job, and now it’s the bowlers’ turn to take responsibility,” he concluded.

briefs.headline: Ranji Trophy: Badoni, Mathur mastermind a perfect day for Delhi
briefs.deck: The skipper extends his purple patch with an unbeaten 210; the No. 7 batter hits an unconquered 150 during their unbroken 334-run sixth-wicket alliance as the visitor posts a mammoth total
briefs.bodyText:
The best batters have the capacity to operate a gear or two below their optimum and still compile runs in the Ranji Trophy as inevitably as a tide returning to shore. Ayush Badoni’s double century on day two of Delhi’s Elite Group C clash against Jharkhand conveyed that feeling.
Such was the measured manner in which the Delhi skipper registered an unbeaten 210 in his team’s imposing first-innings total of 515 for five declared at the JSCA International Stadium here on Tuesday.
The 26-year-old may not spring to mind as one of the most prolific run-scorers going around in India’s domestic system, but his numbers speak glowingly of his growing appetite. It was Badoni’s second successive double century, backing up his career-best effort of 217 in Delhi’s previous round against Gujarat.
Sumit Mathur was equally deserving of the spotlight. The southpaw stayed unconquered on 150, forging an uninterrupted 334-run stand with Badoni. From the moment both batters resumed at 309 for five, the runs flowed like a torrent down a steep hill.
Jharkhand’s bowlers looked so rudderless that Badoni and Mathur could have easily unlocked more personal milestones, but the visitors took the aggressive route by declaring midway through the second session.
The decision was justified as Delhi’s attack found greater help from the pitch and reduced the host to 131 for four at stumps. Utkarsh Singh’s unbeaten 53 off 129 balls, containing crisp punches through point, was the lone act of defiance in reply.
In just the second over, seamer Dev Lakra elicited a poke from Aryaman Sen outside off-stump for Yash Dhull to grab at first slip. The spinners also stepped up, with Hrithik Shokeen, Badoni and debutant left-arm slow bowler Aman Chaudhary snaring a wicket apiece.
The latter’s maiden First Class scalp, which came with 10 minutes left when Virat Singh’s lap-sweep lobbed to short-leg, was the perfect end to a flawless day for Delhi.

briefs.headline: 13-goal blitz! India show no mercy as Mandeep runs riot at ACT hockey tournament
briefs.deck: India began their Asian Champions Trophy title defence with a crushing 13-0 victory over Bangladesh. Mandeep Singh scored a hat-trick, while Harmanpreet Singh, Dilpreet Singh and Hardik Singh netted twice each. India dominated from start to finish, leading 6-0 at half-time. The defending champions will next face China on Thursday, while Bangladesh prepare to take on Malaysia.
briefs.bodyText:
Five-time champions India began their title defence at the Asian Champions Trophy hockey tournament in style, crushing Bangladesh 13-0 at the Olympian Surjit Singh Hockey Stadium on Tuesday. Mandeep Singh led the charge with a hat-trick, while captain 
Harmanpreet Singh
, Dilpreet Singh and 
Hardik Singh
 scored two goals each.
India dominated the match from the beginning, keeping most of the play inside Bangladesh’s half. Harmanpreet opened the scoring in the second minute with a powerful flick from a penalty corner. A minute later, Mandeep doubled the lead after receiving a clever pass from the skipper. Mandeep scored again in the 10th minute, while Shilanand Lakra made it 4-0 just before the first quarter ended.
India continued their attacking display in the second quarter, with Abhishek scoring in the 18th minute and Nilakanta Sharma adding another goal in the 26th minute. Despite a few good saves by Bangladesh goalkeeper Ashraful Shad, India went into half-time with a comfortable 6-0 lead.
India’s goal fest continues
The third quarter saw India increase the pressure further. Dilpreet Singh scored twice within a minute, finding the net first from a rebound and then with a powerful tomahawk shot. 
Harmanpreet soon added his second goal of the match from a penalty corner, taking India’s tally to nine.
Jugraj Singh scored early in the final quarter, before Mandeep completed his hat-trick in the 54th minute with a diving deflection. Hardik Singh then struck twice in the closing moments, scoring once from a rebound and once from open play to complete the 13-0 rout.
The match also witnessed an unusual interruption when a stray dog entered the pitch and pooped on the turf, briefly delaying the start of the second quarter.
